overview.text: Topology is a branch of mathematics that studies spaces and the features they retain under continuous change. A useful picture is to imagine stretching or twisting a shape without tearing it, though topology also has a formal language for spaces and continuity beyond physical shapes. It focuses on properties such as connectivity rather than measurements like exact length or angles. For example, a circle and an ellipse are topologically equivalent. Topology is significant because its ideas help mathematicians compare many kinds of spaces, including surfaces and knots, and its concepts of continuity are used across mathematics.

key_facts.text: In the intuitive “rubber-sheet” view, stretching and twisting are allowed, but tearing is not; this is a guide to the subject, not its full formal definition.
A circle and an ellipse are topologically equivalent, as are a sphere and an ellipsoid: their exact dimensions and outlines differ, but their topological properties match.
Topological invariants include features such as connectivity and dimension—properties used to distinguish spaces even when measurements like distance are set aside.
Topology also studies how one object sits inside another; knot theory grew from questions about such relationships.
Topology includes areas such as general, geometric, algebraic, and differential topology, and its concepts of continuity are used throughout mathematics.
